senses.def: a tree regarded by some (though probably wrongly) as the ancestor of the domestic olive tree; smaller, produces smaller fruit with less oil than domestic variety; Olea europaea sylvestris
senses.comment: In speaking of the wild olive tree as ‘an uncultivated olive tree,’ it is important to make clear that it is not the matter of neglect which produces the wild tree, but the fact that such a tree is essentially different from the cultivated one. A marginal note to this effect may be useful in the context of Romans 11:17. The precise identification of the ‘wild olive tree’ cannot be made with certainty. It may be possible in some instances to speak of such a tree as an ‘uncultivated olive tree’ in contrast with a ‘cultivated olive tree.’ It may also be possible to speak of the wild olive tree as ‘the olive tree producing bitter fruit,’ although in reality all olives are bitter before they are cured.|This reference in Romans 11:17 is intentionally strange because the usual course of action was to graft cultivated branches into wild trees.

senses.def: (derivative of Αἰθιωπία ‘Ethiopia,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Ethiopia
pertaining to strict conformity to a norm or standard, involving both detail and completeness
the capture or catching of animals
to cause oneself to be recognized or to be known again
to cause people to riot against
to cause something to become loose
to desert or forsake a person and thus leave that individual uncared for
to stop doing something, with the implication of complete cessation
pertaining to having a relatively high degree of comparable merit or worth
pertaining to being fitting or proper in corresponding to what should be expected
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπογίνομαι ‘to die,’ not occurring in the NT) to cease, with a complete and abrupt change
senses.comment: It is possible that in the translation of this phrase in 1 Peter 2:24 one might wish to preserve the figurative form and translate as ‘dying to sin.’ For another interpretation of ἀπογίνομαι in 1 Peter 2:24, see 74.27.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπογίνομαι ‘to die,’ not occurring in the NT) to be unable to respond or react to any impulse or desire
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of ‘dying to sin.’ In some instances one can preserve the figurative meaning by an expression such as ‘to be like dead as far as desiring to sin’ or ‘to be like a corpse as far as temptations to sin are concerned.’|For another interpretation of ἀπογίνομαι in 1 Peter 2:24, see 68.40.

senses.def: a written statement prepared by a husband and given to a wife as evidence of a legal divorce
pertaining to being to the left of some point of reference
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 6:7 the phrase ὅπλον ἀριστερόν, literally ‘left-hand weapon,’ refers to a weapon used by the left hand and therefore a defensive weapon, while ὅπλον δεξιόν, literally ‘weapon for the right hand,’ refers to an offensive weapon.|For an interpretation of ἀριστερός as part of an idiom in Mark 10:37, see 87.35.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.comment: The left hand is designated in a number of languages by an idiomatic phrase which normally contrasts with expressions for the right hand. For example, one may often speak of the left hand as ‘the bad hand’ or ‘the weak hand,’ and in some instances as ‘the anus hand,’ since this is the hand used in cleansing the body after defecation. See also 8.32.

senses.def: the Roman province of Asia, primarily the western part of present-day Turkey
to increase in the extent of or in the instances of an activity or state
senses.comment: If one assumes that ἐπίγνωσις in Colossians 1:10 is to be understood in the sense of ‘knowledge about’ (see 28.18), then one may translate this expression as ‘you will know more and more about God,’ but if ἐπίγνωσις is to be understood in the sense of ‘to experience knowledge’ (see 28.2), one may ‘you will know God more and more’ or ‘you will come to know more and more what God does.’

senses.def: to cause something to increase
to grow, to increase in size, whether of animate beings or of plants
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must make a clear distinction in the choice of terms referring to the growth of an animate being (animal or human) and the growth of plants.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: to increase in status
glosses: to enjoy greater respect or honor
senses.comment: In some languages the increase or decrease of respect or honor must be expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘he must become more of a chief while I become more of a follower’ or ‘he must become a big man while I become a small man.’

senses.def: to increase in the degree of a state
senses.comment: It would be possible to interpret αὐξάνομαι in 2 Corinthians 10:15 as being quantitative, but with an expression of state such as πίστις, intensity of degree seems to be more appropriate. In a number of languages, however, it may be necessary to render this expression in 2 Corinthians 10:15 as ‘hoping that you may trust more and more.’

senses.def: a standing in society implying rank or status
to control the activity of someone, based presumably upon correct judgment and decision
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘the peace of Christ’ as ‘controlling.’ In some instances one may translate this expression in Colossians 3:15 as ‘the peace that Christ provides should show you what you should think.’

senses.def: coming into existence by birth
senses.comment: A literal translation of Matthew 1:18 as ‘this is the way that Jesus Christ was born’ might be misleading, since it would imply a description of the actual process of his birth rather than an account of those circumstances and events which took place in connection with his birth. It may, therefore, be better to translate Matthew 1:18 as ‘this is what happened when Jesus Christ was born’ or ‘these things happened at the time of Jesus Christ’s birth.’

senses.def: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
senses.comment: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις[b], οἶκος[c], and πατριά[a] is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις in Matthew 1:1 as being part of what is essentially a title for the book of Matthew and thus would render the introductory phrase as ‘the book of the history of Jesus Christ’ (see γένεσις[c] ‘history,’ 33.19).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).

senses.def: an account of the origin and life of someone
senses.comment: For the most part, scholars understand the phrase βίβλος γενέσεως in Matthew 1:1 as referring to the list of ancestors which immediately follows. Therefore, βίβλος γενέσεως is more often interpreted as ‘the record of the ancestors’ or ‘the birth record of …’ (see 10.24).

senses.def: the state of existence
senses.comment: In James 1:23 the term γένεσις is largely redundant, for the reference could only be to a person’s own face.

senses.def: (derivative of δαιμόνιον[a] ‘demon,’ 12.37) to be possessed by a demon
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of a person ‘being possessed by a demon.’ A more appropriate expression may be ‘the person possesses a demon.’ In other instances an idiomatic phrase is employed, ‘the demon rides the person’ or ‘the demon commands the person’ or even ‘the demon is the person.’

senses.def: (derivative of δεσμός[b] ‘to be in prison,’ 37.115) a person who is under custody in prison
to distribute objects to a series of persons
glosses: to give to each in turn

senses.def: to be divided into opposing and hostile units
to divide into separate parts
senses.comment: For another interpretation of διαμερίζω in Acts 2:3 (as middle, not passive), see 15.140.

senses.def: to disperse, on the basis of having been divided up
senses.comment: There are, however, serious questions as to the precise meaning of διαμερίζομαι in Acts 2:3; the meaning could be ‘tongues as of fire dispersing one to each person,’ but it is also possible that the individual tongues of fire were divided (see 63.23).

senses.def: to translate from one language to another
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to translate’ or ‘to interpret’ is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘it comes out in our language as’ or ‘in our words it means’ or ‘in our mouths it says.’

senses.def: to explain on a more extensive and formal level the meaning of something which is particularly obscure or difficult to comprehend
(derivative of δίδωμι[a] ‘to give,’ 57.71) that which is given
one who guarantees the reality of something
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
senses.comment: In view of the fact that εἰσδέχομαι in 2 Corinthians 6:17 refers to God’s receiving people, it may be necessary to use quite a different expression than one would normally employ in referring to welcoming a guest into the home. In some instances one may use a rather generic expression such as ‘to accept,’ and this may be expressed idiomatically in some languages as ‘to extend my hand to you’ or ‘to count you as belonging to me.’ It is the figurative usage of εἰσδέχομαι in this type of context which may lead to a somewhat different type of rendering.

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a special choice based upon significant preference, often implying a strongly favorable attitude toward what is chosen

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: (semantic derivative of ἐκλογή[a] ‘choice,’ 30.92) that which has been chosen
to state that someone has done wrong, with the implication that there is adequate proof of such wrongdoing

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.def: to spit on or at something or someone
senses.comment: In some societies spitting has quite a different symbolic meaning than it has in the Western world. In fact, in some societies in Africa, to spit upon a person’s head is to confer a blessing. It may therefore be necessary in the case of Matthew 26:67 to translate ‘they spat in his face’ as ‘they spat in his face to dishonor him’ or ‘… to show their anger against him.’

senses.def: (derivative of ἐντέλλομαι ‘to command,’ 33.329) that which is authoritatively commanded
to indicate agreement with a proposition or offer
senses.comment: In some languages one may render ‘he agreed to it’ by simply saying ‘he said, I will do it.’

senses.def: to express openly one’s allegiance to a proposition or person
senses.comment: It is often extremely difficult, if not impossible, to translate ὁμολογέω[a], ὁμολογία, and ἐξομολογέω[b] by the usual expression for ‘confess,’ since this would usually imply that one has done something wrong. It is normally necessary, therefore, to employ quite a different type of relationship, usually involving a public utterance and an expression of confidence or allegiance. For example, in Matthew 10:32 it may be necessary to translate ‘whoever tells people publicly that he is loyal to me, I will tell my Father that I am loyal to that person.’ Similarly, in Hebrews 10:23 one may translate ‘let us hold on to the hope in which we have told people we have such confidence.’ Likewise, in Romans 15:9 one may translate ‘therefore I will tell the Gentiles how I have put my confidence in you.’|For another interpretation of ἐξομολογέομαι in Romans 15:9, see 33.359.

senses.def: to acknowledge a fact publicly, often in reference to previous bad behavior
senses.comment: In Philippians 2:11 the statement πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται ὅτι κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός (‘that everyone may confess that Jesus Christ is Lord’) means simply to acknowledge a fact publicly, and in this instance there is no implication of previous bad behavior.|In translating Matthew 3:6 in some languages, it may be useful to restructure the expression somewhat, for example, ‘they admitted to people that they had sinned’ or ‘they admitted publicly to God …’

senses.def: to acknowledge one’s thankfulness, restricted in NT usage to contexts in which God is the one being thanked
to express praise or honor, with a possible implication of acknowledging the nature of someone or something (occurring in the NT only in quotations from the Septuagint)
senses.comment: This meaning of ἐξομολογέομαι is almost guaranteed by the parallelism of the second line of the quotation in Romans 15:9, but for another interpretation of Romans 15:9, see 33.274.

senses.def: to move to or on to, generally with the implication of having arrived
senses.comment: In the rendering of Luke 1:35 it is important to avoid the kind of literal translation which might suggest sexual relations.

senses.def: to use sudden physical force against someone as the outgrowth of a hostile attitude
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to attack’ is simply ‘to start fighting against.’ In some languages, however, the equivalent is ‘to jump on’ or ‘to grab to do harm to.’

senses.def: to happen to someone or something, with the implication of an event which is undesirable
to press or push against
to happen suddenly to, with the connotation of something bad and adverse
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘insults happening.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to restructure this expression in Romans 15:3 as ‘they began insulting me in the same way they used to insult you.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to fall on the neck) to show special affection for by throwing one’s arms around a person
senses.comment: A literal translation of ἐπιπίπτω ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον ‘to fall on someone’s neck’ can be seriously misunderstood. In fact, in some languages it is so close to an expression meaning ‘to kill’ that one should normally avoid any literal rendering. At the same time, it is very important not to employ terms for ‘embrace’ and ‘kiss’ in Acts 20:37 which might suggest improper sexual interests.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: as to speak a word) an expression used to introduce an alternative form of expression as an interpretation of what has been said
a Christian who sent greetings in 2 Timothy 4:21
to produce an abundance of good fruit or grain
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult, if not impossible, to speak of the ground producing crops (Luke 12:16). Therefore, one may employ such expressions as ‘good crops grew on the ground’ or ‘the plants produced plenty of fruit’ or ‘… plenty of grain.’

senses.def: a marker of an alternative
a marker of comparison
a marker of double alternatives
a female deity
senses.comment: In some languages it may seem quite strange to attribute female sex to a divine being. However, one can almost always say ‘a woman god’ or ‘a spirit like a woman’ or ‘a spirit thought of as being like a woman.’

senses.def: a city in Lycaonia
a person in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: one who customarily engages in doing what is bad
to cause serious trouble to, with the implication of dire consequences and probably a weakened state
to cause to be thoroughly prepared
to make or erect any kind of construction
(an idiom, literally: to prepare the road) to cause circumstances to be ready or propitious for some event
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to render this expression in Matthew 11:10 as ‘who will arrange everything for you.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be seared in the conscience, or: to be seared as to one’s conscience) to be unwilling to learn from one’s conscience
glosses: to refuse to listen to one’s conscience

senses.def: a Christian woman who sent greetings in 2 Timothy 4:21
to apply whitewash to a surface
senses.comment: For many languages the closest equivalent of the phrase ‘whitewashed tombs’ is simply ‘tombs that have been painted white.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: whitewashed wall) one who pretends to be one thing, while in reality he is something quite different

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: a very hard, translucent, and usually transparent type of quartz
senses.comment: The equivalent of ‘crystal’ is often a descriptive phrase such as ‘a brilliant stone’ or ‘a shining stone’ or ‘a glass-like stone.’ In developing a satisfactory term for crystal, it is important to avoid possible confusion with diamond.|Some scholars, however, interpret κρύσταλλος in Revelation 4:6 as being a reference to ice (see 2.11).

senses.def: frozen water
senses.comment: In both Revelation 4:6 and Revelation 22:1 (the only two passages in which κρύσταλλος occurs in the NT) the meaning may, however, be ‘rock crystal’ rather than ‘ice’ (see 2.46).|Though in the Arctic regions people may have a number of different terms for various kinds and forms of ice, there are many areas in the world in which there is no existing local term for ‘ice.’ Sometimes a descriptive phrase such as ‘hardened water’ is employed, and in a number of languages a term is simply borrowed from a dominant language of the region. However, in Revelation 4:6 and Revelation 22:1 it is possible to focus upon the brilliance of color rather than the particular substance and thus to speak of λαμπρὸς ὡς κρύσταλλος as ‘that which is sparkling white’ or ‘… bright white.’

senses.def: pertaining to having been hewn out of rock
senses.comment: In Luke 23:53 ‘rock’ must be understood as a basic outcropping of rock, so that the grave would have been a cave-like structure cut into a rock outcropping.

senses.def: to think about something in a detailed and logical manner
fallacious and deceptive reasoning and, by implication, based on evil intentions
senses.comment: It may be difficult in some languages to speak of ‘false arguments,’ especially if the equivalent of ‘arguments’ is a verb meaning ‘to argue’ or ‘to discuss against someone.‘ One can, however, express the semantic content of ‘false arguments’ (as reflected in λογισμός[b]) by translating as ‘what people say when they argue, but their words are not true’ or ‘they argue with words that are not true.’

senses.def: a position at a relatively great distance from another position
senses.comment: For εἰς in Acts 2:39, see 84.16).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a person who habitually drinks too much and thus becomes a drunkard
to share in the possession of something

(normally occurring together with a term specifying the particular food in question, but also occurring absolutely in contexts relating to food; μετέχω[b] is probably more formal than ἐσθίω[a], 23.1) to partake of or to consume food, whether solid or liquid
senses.comment: In contexts in which μετέχω occurs, it may be important to select a term for the eating which will go specifically with the type of food in question. For various types of distinctions made in terms for eating, see the discussion at 23.1 and its footnote.

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: to be included in the membership of a group
senses.comment: In order to express the meaning of ‘belonged to a different tribe,’ it may be necessary to say ‘he had a different tribe name’ or ‘his tribe was different’ or ‘he was counted as a member of another tribe.’

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to share in a table) to belong to a particular religious group as evidenced by ceremonial eating
glosses: to eat at the table of

senses.def: to promise a person for marriage
senses.comment: It may be important to note in the margin of a text that in biblical times the act of betrothal was regarded as binding, so that the breaking of a betrothal was legally equivalent to divorce.

senses.def: a person whose household is greeted in Romans 16:11
the state of being diseased
one who owns and manages a household, including family, servants, and slaves
the young of a donkey ὄνος
senses.comment: As in the case of ὄνος ‘donkey’ (4.31), a number of languages make a distinction either in form or in terms for the young of a donkey based upon distinctions in sex.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the quality of holiness as an expression of the divine in contrast with the human
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὁσιότης in Luke 1:75, see 53.45.

senses.def: the state resulting from being dedicated to the service of God
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὁσιότης in Luke 1:75, see 88.25.

senses.def: to provide instruction, with the intent of forming proper habits of behavior
to train someone in accordance with proper rules of conduct and behavior
to punish for the purpose of improved behavior
to conform in one’s behavior to a particular system of instruction or teaching
(a figurative extension of meaning of παρακολουθέω ‘to follow,’ not occurring in the NT) to make an extensive effort to learn the details and truth about something
to happen in conjunction with some other happening
glosses: to happen at the same time

senses.def: to live or dwell temporari ly in a place as a stranger
to dwell more or less permanently in a place which is not one’s own country (compare related meanings in 11.7.)
cardinal number, where there are five instances of a countable entity
to refuse to recognize the force or power of something
to increase greatly in number or extent
senses.comment: It may be difficult to speak of ‘a number growing’ in some languages, so that one may need to translate this expression in Acts 6:7 as ‘the disciples in Jerusalem became more and more’ or ‘there were more and more disciples in Jerusalem.’|It may be difficult, if not impossible, to speak of ‘evil increasing’ as in Matthew 24:12, but one can usually speak of a greater number of instances of doing evil, and therefore one may translate ‘more and more people will be doing what is evil.’|A literal rendering of Acts 12:24 may be impossible in many languages, for a strictly literal rendering would imply that somehow the message from God ‘got bigger,’ which may mean in some languages ‘resulted in lies.’ The meaning is, of course, that more and more people accepted God’s word as true.

senses.def: to cause an increase in the number of objects
senses.comment: In Hebrews 6:14 it is essential in most languages to specify what is increased. A strictly literal translation such as ‘to cause you to increase’ would simply mean ‘to cause you to get big.’ The reference is clearly to Abraham’s descendants, and it is usually essential to make this reference clear.

senses.def: to begin vegetative growth, with special emphasis upon the sprouting of leaves
senses.comment: The initial stages of growth, either of a plant as a whole or in the renewal of foliage after a winter or dry season, may be expressed in a number of ways, for example, ‘to become green again,’ ‘to show leaves,’ ‘to see leaves begin,’ or ‘when leaves unfold.’

senses.def: to stretch out or to spread out an object
senses.comment: In a number of languages one would not speak of a person being ‘stretched out’ in order to be whipped, but merely ‘tied up’ or ‘tied in a stretched-out position.’

senses.def: fiery red (probably with a tinge of yellow or orange)
senses.comment: As in other instances of color terms, it may be necessary in Revelation 6:4 to use an expression which is particularly applicable to a horse.

senses.def: in the Latin language
the port city of Antioch in Syria

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being obdurate and obstinate
senses.comment: In the contexts illustrated by σκληροτράχηλος, ἀπερίτμητος καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, and σκληροκαρδία, the focus of the stubbornness and obstinacy is the unwillingness to be taught or to understand.

senses.def: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy
to do something with intense effort and motivation

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
(an idiom, literally: to bring every effort to) to do one’s very best in attempting to do something
glosses: to try as hard as possible
senses.comment: In some languages it may be almost impossible to speak of ‘adding goodness to faith’ (2 Peter 1:5). However, an appropriate equivalent of this expression may be ‘do your best to be good as well as to believe.’

senses.def: an upright shaft or structure used as a building support
senses.comment: στῦλος is also used in speaking of the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9; see 36.7). In Galatians 2:9 the focus is upon the important role of such persons in supporting and maintaining the church. In a number of languages such a figurative meaning may be expressed as ‘very important persons in the church.’|In a number of languages pillars may be described as ‘those poles which support the house’ or ‘those logs which hold up the roof.’ Usually, however, there are rather specific terms to designate these important parts in the construction of houses or halls.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of στῦλος[a] ‘pillar, column,’ 7.45) one who is a leader of a group, with the implication of strategic responsibility
pertaining to that which has a similar form or nature
senses.comment: In the case of Romans 8:29 it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘he set them apart in order that they might be like his Son,’ and in Philippians 3:21 it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘having a glorious body like his.’

senses.def: one who is away from home on a journey with someone else
(a figurative extension of meaning of συστρατιώτης ‘fellow soldier,’ not occurring in the NT) one who serves in arduous tasks or undergoes severe experiences together with someone else
glosses: one who works arduously along with
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of συστρατιώτης in Philemon 1:2 might imply that Paul himself was a soldier and therefore, in a sense, a secret agent of some military force. Accordingly, it may be necessary to employ a simile, for example, ‘who works like a fellow soldier’ or ‘one who experiences great hardships along with us.’

senses.def: a place for burying
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand ταφή in the context of Matthew 27:7 as a reference to the process of burial, and one may therefore translate Matthew 27:7 as ‘they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field to bury foreigners.’

senses.def: (derivative of τίμιος[a] ‘valuable, precious,’ 65.2) a large quantity of costly, valuable possessions
senses.comment: ‘Wealth’ may usually be rendered by ‘the many valuable possessions.’

senses.def: Asiatic Rock dove: bird with a blue-gray color with a pinkish sheen to the neck feathers and a black tip on its tail; lives in large colonies and eats mainly seeds; courts, mates, and has nests several times a year; nests on rock ledges; Columba via; used as food and for sacrifices; regarded as swift, docile, and innocent
senses.comment: Though in English a relatively clear distinction is made between ‘doves’ (which have pointed tails) and ‘pigeons’ (which have square off tails), there seems to be no such distinction in the use of περιστερά and τρυγών in the Greek of the New Testament.|There are, however, certain problems involved in the connotations of terms relating to pigeons or doves. According to ancient zoology, the dove was thought to have no bile, and consequently, therefore, to be a very peaceful and clean bird. It thus became a symbol of Christian virtue and of gentleness (as in Matthew 10:16). In reality, however, doves and pigeons are quite aggressive, and a group of pigeons are frequently known to peck an injured bird to death. Therefore, in some societies pigeons or doves are not regarded as gentle or peaceful, but rather as wicked and harmful. In fact, in some cultures doves are thought to be symbols of death and of evil. Under such circumstances it is important, therefore, to have some marginal note so as to indicate clearly the symbolic significance of such birds in biblical contexts.

senses.def: an extraordinary degree, involving a considerable excess over what would be expected (this series differs from the series in 78.31 primarily in emphasizing the excessive degree)
to sail or move along beside some object which provides a degree of protection or shelter
glosses: to sail under the shelter of

senses.def: a city in the west central part of Asia Minor
(derivative of the base φρον ‘thoughtful planning,’ 26.15) to employ one’s faculty for thoughtful planning, with emphasis upon the underlying disposition or attitude
glosses: to think in a particular manner
senses.comment: In some instances it may be appropriate to render Philippians 2:5 as ‘you should think the way Christ Jesus did’ or ‘how Jesus Christ thought about things is the way you should think about them’ (in which a term meaning ‘things’ would refer to events and not simply to material objects).|It is also possible to understand φρονέω in Philippians 2:5 as referring specifically to the attitude of people to one another.

senses.def: to keep on giving serious consideration to something
glosses: to let one’s mind dwell on

senses.subdomain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View
senses.def: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to acknowledge the high status of a person or event

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have an arrogant, haughty attitude
(a figurative extension of meaning of χάσμα ‘yawning,’ not occurring in the NT) a deep, unbridgeable valley or trough between two points
senses.comment: In this only NT occurrence of χάσμα the reference is to the impassable space between two parts of the supernatural abode of the dead. Translators frequently use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a deep valley which no one may cross’ or ‘a space which cannot be crossed.’

senses.def: (derivative of χρυσός[a] ‘gold,’ 2.49) pertaining to being made or consisting of gold
the state of having acquired an advantage or benefit
